rubella.x: They have congenital rubella syndrome, which they acquired during an outbreak of the rubella virus, or German measles.

ruble.e: Borrowed from Russian рубль (rublʹ). Doublet of rubel and rubl.

rubric.e: From Middle English rubriche, rubrike, from Old French rubrique, from Latin rūbrīca (“red ochre”), the substance used to make red letters, from ruber (“red”), from…
rubric.x: That would fall under the rubric of things we can ignore for now.

ruckus.e: Recorded since 1890; probably a blend of ruction (“disturbance”) + rumpus (“disturbance, fracas”) - potentially with influence from raucous (“rowdy, hoarse”), from Latin…

rudder.x: For rhyme the rudder is of verses,/With which, like ships, they steer their courses.

rudely.e: From Middle English rudely, rudeliche, equivalent to rude + -ly.

rudeness.e: From Middle English rudenesse, equivalent to rude + -ness.
rudeness.x: The rudeness of the cabin gave it a rustic charm but little comfort.

rudimentary.x: I have only a rudimentary grasp of chemistry.

ruffian.e: From Middle French rufian, from Italian ruffiano (“pimp”).
ruffian.x: What wilt thou on thy death-bed play the Ruffian?

ruffle.e: From Middle English ruffelen, perhaps from Old Norse hrufla (“to graze, scratch”) or Middle Low German ruffelen (“to wrinkle, curl”). Further origin unknown.
ruffle.x: She loved the dress with the lace ruffle at the hem.

rugby.e: From the name of Rugby School in Rugby, in Warwickshire, England, United Kingdom, where the modern game was developed in the 19th century.

rugged.e: From Middle English rugged, roggyd, ruggyd, derived from Old Norse rǫgg (“tuft, shagginess”), equivalent to rug (“rough, woollen material”) + -ed.
rugged.x: BY and by, after a rugged climb, we halted on the summit of a hill which commanded a far-reaching view.

ruler.e: From Middle English reuler; equivalent to rule + -er.

rumble.e: From Middle English rumblen, romblen, rummelyn, frequentative form of romen (“to roar”), equivalent to rome + -le.
rumble.x: The rumble from passing trucks made it hard to sleep at night.

ruminate.e: First attested in 1533; borrowed from Latin rūminātus, perfect active participle of rūminor (“to chew the cud, turn over in the mind”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix))…
ruminate.x: A camel will ruminate just as a cow will.

rumination.e: From Latin rūminātio (“chewing the cud”); see ruminate.

rummage.e: From Middle English ronage, from Old French arrumage (compare French arrimage), from arrumer (“to arrange the cargo in the hold”) (compare French arrimer and Spanish…
rummage.x: After the long voyage, the customs officers rummaged the ship.

rummy.e: Unknown, with much speculation. Perhaps related to rum via poker slang, or ultimately from German Ruhm (“fame, glory”).

runaway.x: Runaways are vulnerable to criminal exploitation.

runic.x: Then flowered the mead, then leafed all 'Twas caused by the runic lay.

runner.e: From Middle English rennere, rynner, urnare, equivalent to run + -er. Cognate with Old Norse rennari (“runner; messenger”).
runner.x: The first runner to cross the finish line wins the race.

runoff.x: The runoff of nitrates is poisoning the lake.

runway.x: A TAKE-DOWN CANOE RUNWAY. A very handy adjunct to the camp of a canoeist is a runway that can be taken apart and transported easily.

rupee.e: Coined by Sher Shah Suri, the Sultan of the Suri Empire 1540–1545 as Hindustani रुपीया / رُوپِییَہ (rūpīya), variant of रुपया / رُوپَیَہ (rūpaya, “rupee”), from Sanskrit…

rupture.x: Hatch from the egg, that soon, / Bursting with kindly rupture, forth disclosed / Their callow young.

rural.e: From Old French rural, from Latin rūrālis (“rural”), from rūs (“countryside”) + -ālis.

rusalka.e: From Russian руса́лка (rusálka, “mermaid, siren”). Doublet of rosalia.
rusalka.x: She is now a rusalka, a water spirit; in revenge she sends their daughter, a rusalochka, to lure him into the water.

russet.e: From Middle English russet, from Anglo-Norman russet, rossat, roset, and Middle French rosset, rousset (“reddish, reddish-brown.

rutabaga.e: First attested in 1799, borrowed from Swedish rotabagge, a dialectal word from Västergötland, from rot (“root”) + bagge (“lump, bunch”).
rutabaga.x: American kids ate very odd things in the 19th century. Spicy sauces and vinegary pickles. Shellfish and organ meats. Beets, rutabagas, collards.
